Malaysia Lifts Temporary Export Ban on Oil & Gas Producers, Industry Operations Resume

KUALA LUMPUR – The Malaysian government has lifted a temporary export ban on crude oil and natural gas products, bringing relief to the country’s Oil & Gas Producers industry after weeks of uncertainty. The measure, which was enacted last month in response to concerns over domestic supply stability, had restricted the export of key petroleum products and liquefied natural gas (LNG), impacting several major players including Southern Gas Trading JSC.

Industry officials confirmed yesterday that the ban was officially rescinded following a review by the Ministry of International Trade and Industry, which determined that domestic reserves had stabilized. According to the ministry’s statement, “Malaysia’s strategic stockpiles are now deemed sufficient to meet both local demand and international commitments. The government remains committed to ensuring stability and reliability in the sector.”

Southern Gas Trading JSC, one of the companies directly affected by the ban, announced the immediate resumption of export activities from its Bintulu terminal. “We are grateful for the government’s swift response in reviewing the policy,” said company spokesperson Noraini Zulkifli. “Our teams are working around the clock to fulfill pending contracts and restore our export schedules.”

The export ban, which came into force in mid-May, caused a temporary halt in overseas shipments and prompted concerns among industry stakeholders regarding potential revenue losses and contractual penalties. “The month-long restriction placed significant pressure on our export operations,” said Mohd Azmi Rahman, President of the Malaysian Oil & Gas Producers Association. “We estimate that the industry collectively faced a reduction of up to 15% in monthly export volumes during the period.”

Analysts note that while the disruption was brief, it highlighted the importance of clear communication and contingency planning within the industry. “Producers had to quickly adapt to shifting policy directives and manage relationships with international buyers,” said energy analyst Liew Chee Seng. “Fortunately, the swift resolution has minimized long-term impacts.”

With the ban now lifted, export terminals across Malaysia have resumed operations, and companies are ramping up shipments to meet delayed orders. Industry observers expect export volumes to normalize by early July, as producers work to make up for lost time and reaffirm Malaysia’s position in the regional energy market.
